title: Social protection has expanded at historic scale but coverage, benefit adequacy, and delivery infrastructure still leave billions exposed to shocks
source_unit: World Bank, State of Social Protection Report 2025: The 2-Billion-Person Challenge
geography: Low- and middle-income countries, with comparisons by income group, region, poverty status, gender, and social-protection function

observations.period: 2010-2022; expansion of social protection and labor programs

denominator.unit: low- and middle-income country population coverage frame

people_reached.unit: people gaining access to social protection and labor programs over the past decade, as reported by the World Bank

coverage_2010.unit: percent of the population covered in 2010

coverage_2022.unit: percent of the population covered in 2022

expansion_boundary.value: historic expansion coexists with large uncovered and inadequately covered populations

observations.method: World Bank synthesis using ASPIRE administrative indicators and household-survey evidence on social assistance, social insurance, and labor-market programs.
observations.uncertainty: Coverage aggregates different programs and definitions across countries and years; access to a program does not establish regular receipt, adequacy, or effective protection.
observations.subgroup: Poor households, workers, older people, children, women, people with disabilities, and populations in low- and middle-income countries.
observations.counterinterpretation: The ten-percentage-point increase represents substantial institutional progress even though it falls short of universal and adequate protection.

denominator.unit: people in low- and middle-income countries with no or inadequate social protection coverage

inadequately_covered.unit: people remaining uncovered or inadequately covered

low_income_no_coverage.unit: percent of people in low-income countries receiving no form of social protection

benefit_adequacy.unit: people whose benefits are so meager they may not help escape poverty or cushion unexpected shocks

poor_household_transfer.unit: percent of poor-household income represented by social-assistance transfers in low-income countries

observations.method: World Bank coverage and adequacy synthesis by country income group, poverty status, and social-protection benefit level.
observations.uncertainty: The estimates combine country data with different reference years, program definitions, and measurement quality; adequacy is not identical to household welfare or resilience.
observations.subgroup: People in extreme poverty, poor households, low-income countries, fragile and conflict-affected regions, and recipients of low-value benefits.
observations.counterinterpretation: Even small benefits can protect consumption or preserve human capital at critical moments, while adequacy may improve through complementary services and labor opportunities.

observations.period: 2020; emergency social protection response during the COVID-19 pandemic

emergency_reach.unit: people reached by emergency social-protection responses in developing countries

delivery_infrastructure.value: countries with robust delivery infrastructure before the pandemic responded more effectively

shock_response_tools.value: databases, digital payments, case management, and early-warning systems are identified as infrastructure for timely support

observations.method: World Bank synthesis of pandemic social-protection responses and the pre-existing systems that enabled rapid scale-up.
observations.uncertainty: Reach counts do not measure benefit adequacy, duration, exclusion, or the counterfactual effect of delivery infrastructure; pandemic response patterns may not generalize to every shock.
observations.subgroup: Households and workers exposed to pandemic income loss, informal workers, people without records or payment access, and governments scaling emergency support.
observations.counterinterpretation: Ad hoc responses and community channels can reach people when formal systems are weak, while robust systems may still exclude migrants or people outside administrative databases.

observations.period: 2025; adequacy, gender, labor programs, and path to universal coverage

denominator.unit: countries in the report's gender comparison sample

gender_benefit_ratio.unit: cents received by women in social-protection benefits for every 1 dollar received by men, on average

coverage_timeline_extreme_poverty.unit: years required at current growth rates to achieve full coverage for people living in extreme poverty

coverage_timeline_poorest.unit: years required at current growth rates to cover the poorest 20 percent of households

labor_program_spending.unit: percent of GDP spent on labor-market programs on average

local_multiplier.unit: estimated local-economic multiplier for each dollar transferred to poor families

observations.method: World Bank comparison of benefit adequacy, gender distribution, labor-market-program spending, coverage trajectories, and local economic effects.
observations.uncertainty: Ratios, timelines, and multiplier estimates depend on country samples, program composition, assumptions, and local economic conditions; they are not universal treatment effects.
observations.subgroup: Women benefit recipients, poorest households, labor-market-program participants, local economies, and governments allocating scarce fiscal resources.
observations.counterinterpretation: Improving targeting, program design, labor opportunities, and resource allocation may accelerate coverage and raise effective adequacy without relying only on aggregate spending growth.

related_sources.claim: World Bank ASPIRE provides the social-protection indicators and country comparison context used by the report.
World Bank release summarizes coverage gaps, delivery infrastructure, and policy actions.

boundary: This record adds a global social-protection route across coverage, adequacy, crisis response, delivery infrastructure, gender disparity, labor programs, and household resilience. It uses aggregate World Bank indicators and report synthesis, not respondent-level benefit histories, individual case files, causal transfer effects, household consumption panels, or proof that coverage automatically becomes adequate protection.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official World Bank State of Social Protection 2025 page, summary, ASPIRE context, and release reviewed for coverage expansion, two-billion-person gap, benefit adequacy, pandemic response, gender ratio, timelines, labor-program spending, and policy recommendations.
